Senses.Explanation: The records preserve this place-and-medicine answer to the question 'What is the meaning of winter coming?' and repeatedly quote or cap that exchange. Sushan Kuangren answers the winter question with rhubarb coming from the capital. The geographical and medicinal terms remain explicit.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The book title and enclosing commentary identify Lianfeng as the commenting speaker; the standalone headword is his capping remark.

Senses.Explanation: A winter-melon seal is a crude stamp of certification: it marks people as approved while supplying only the shape of a true seal. Chan masters use the image to attack indiscriminate recognition, formulaic authorization, and premature claims of transmission. Yongjue condemns teachers who stamp one another; Tianyin attacks people determined to stamp students; Tian’an describes seasonal teachers stamping half-ripe practitioners; and Lianfeng caps Huangbo’s threatened blows as the same crude stamp.

Senses.Explanation: To chew over is to find material for conceptual working, verbal rumination, or sustained investigation. Chan records extend the bodily action to sayings and public cases: Yunxi Langting Ting tells beginners to “chew over a ready-made sentence that cannot be knocked down” and repeats “chew it over, chew it over” (咬嚼來、咬嚼去); the same record says Wujin spent his whole life unable to chew through “the bowl-carrying public case” (托缽公案). Other comments use the resistance of food as an explicit comparison: a saying can be “unable to be chewed through” (咬嚼不破), while Donglin offers only “wooden-slat soup and iron-nail rice—chew as you will” (木札羹、鉄釘飯，任汝咬嚼). The record also issues the opposite verdict, “strictly avoid chewing” (切忌咬嚼), after the answer “a thousand-year peach pit.”

Senses.Explanation: The parent image names verbal entanglement in Chan records, but this exact compound is very thin and occurs only in late framing prose. Gao Shitai's prefatory verse praises the record owner for effacing forms and cutting vine-tangle; a preface says that Linji's staff and shout cut all vine-tangle; a biographical preface pairs cutting vine-tangle with destroying thorn thickets. The Zen deviation comes from the established Chan use of creepers for entangling words, here made the object of cutting. Unlike more common longer forms that add an explicit verb of severing, the exact phrase is not attested in this concordance as a live-exchange command, so this entry does not present it as one.

Senses.Explanation: Cutting the cat names Nanquan’s canonical action and functions as a later benchmark for decisive conduct. This graph form occurs 278 times in 119 allowlisted texts and is the orthographic counterpart of “cut the cat” (斬猫), not a different event. In the records it abbreviates the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” the assembly gives no answer, and he cuts the cat in two. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says that had he been there, he would have saved the cat. The phrase functions as case narration and title, an object of questions, a subject for verses, and a cited precedent. One public exchange explicitly asks, “Killing living beings is a major precept; why did Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake?”; Miyun Yuanwu tells the questioner to repent. Another sermon quotes the rule to rescue animals from killing and asks how Nanquan's cat and Guizong's snake could have been saved. These passages establish the corpus's own precept relation without stating Nanquan's intention. Asked for the case's import, Jueyin answers only, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui reports and rejects students' labels “timely wondrous function” and “great function appears, not retaining rules.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 師上堂，拈拄杖示眾云：若向遮裏會去，是頭上安頭；若也不會，又是斬頭覓活。汝等諸人且作麼生承當？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X78/X78n1556.xml). Jianzhong Jingguo Continued Lamp Record. Fachang Yiyu contrasts claiming to understand with adding a head and not understanding with cutting off the head while seeking life.

Senses.Explanation: Cut off the head while seeking life is an impossible rescue: the very act taken to find life removes what must remain alive. Chan masters repeatedly oppose it to adding another head atop one’s own, placing both images on rejected sides of a verbal choice. Poshan applies the pair first to ‘mind/buddha’ wording and again to seeking a decision from oneself or another; Tianyin applies it to saying exertion is absent or present; and Fachang applies it to saying one understands or does not.

Senses.Explanation: A horse's foot, used in Chan exchanges beside the donkey's foot to force or mock a distinction. Masters ask whether a displayed foot is donkey or horse, and reuse the pair when pressing distinctions among apparently equal beings. This is the concrete foot, not yet the idiom for a betrayed flaw.

Senses.Explanation: The telltale flaw by which a position gives itself away. Chan commentators repeatedly say that a forced explanation, a cited answer, or a critical remark has exposed the hidden foot that betrays it. The phrase diagnoses exposure; it does not merely name a horse's anatomy.
